body.html: A Simple Plan

Hollywood invaded Delano in 1998 as the film, “A Simple Plan,” starring Billy Bob Thornton, Bill Paxton, Bridget Fonda, and Laura Dern, was shot in and around the village. Filming was set to begin January 2, but due to a lack of snow the crew was forced to go to Ashland, Wisconsin to film exterior scenes. Parts of the film were also shot in Camp Ihduhapi in Loretto, and at the Moravian church near Victoria, MN.

There were about 65 small Midwestern towns that were being considered as locations for the film, but Delano’s proximity to the Twin Cities helped its being chosen as the location.

Filming in Delano began January 19. Buildings in downtown Delano were given a facelift to create Tippy’s Town Tavern, the Foss Funeral Home, and the Delano Feed and Grain Mill. The Public Library (the Old City Hall) appeared as the Wright County Annex Building, with the interior of the second floor serving as the police station.

The crew came back to Delano in February to reshoot several scenes that had been lost in transport. The Delano Public Works Department had to put snow back on the street, and the city agreed to keep the Christmas decorations up longer than usual because the film takes place around Christmas.
Several residents were cast as extras, and older local cars and trucks from the 70’s and 80’s, rusty and dirty, were requested for the film.
“Area people who appeared as extras in the funeral scene included Laura Murphy, K. J. McDonald, Joe McDonald (as the hearse driver), Dan Reiner, Jerome Andres and Randall Gerhart.”
The film opened in area theaters Friday, January 22, 1999, giving Delano residents the opportunity to see their city on the big screen.
Butch Automatic and the Four Speeds
Popular Local Rock Group

1974 photo

Bob Seliski, Bob Hutter, Dale Graunke, Mike Mathisen, Dave Socher, Brad Bruhn, Dave Pawelk

Butch Automatic and the Four Speeds was formed in 1974 by friends from Delano and Watertown high schools and quickly became one of central and southern Minnesota’s premier rock groups. When Butch Automatic began, its members were music-loving teenagers who looked up to groups like White Sidewalls, The Rockin’ Hollywoods, and Travelin Band Grease Band.

The band’s first members included Bob Hutter, Dave Socher, Mike Mathisen, Bob Seliski, Dale Graunke, Dave Pawelk, and Brad Bruhn. Bob Seliski’s brother, Joe Seliski, joined soon after the band’s start, and vocalist Doreen Shrode was added in the 1990s.

“Butch Automatic was a group of regular guys – with below to average musical talents – who took an idea and worked very hard to create a musical experience that appealed to their audience,” said Joe Seliski in an interview in the Delano Herald Journal, September 3, 2013. “The group added an energy to the music that was not present with other groups.” Dale Graunke added “We were always a theatrical band.”

Butch Automatic has entertained well over half a million people since its inception in 1974, including performing with national acts such as the Monkees, the Trashmen, Tommy and the Shondells, and the Ventures.
Delano Community Theater

The extravagant comedy, “The Womanless Wedding,” was presented January 23 and 24, 1928, in the new high school auditorium, sponsored by the Delano American Legion. Eighty local business and professional men played all the roles. It was reported in the Delano Eagle that “if Delano business institutions suffered a decline for a few days, it was because the proprietors were taking time off to discuss the latest styles in feather fans, high-heeled slippers and evening gowns.” Following the presentation of the rollicking farce, the Eagle stated that the town had been “scoured in search of high-heeled pumps, slippers, party dresses, hats and lingerie to fit the staid businessmen, who blossomed forth as stately matrons, vampires, fashions plates, flappers and country maids.” The play was a huge success, with the performances attended by about 1300 people.

“The Womanless Wedding” was again presented in Delano January 15, 1943, this time sponsored by the Delano Sportsmen’s Club. All of the proceeds from the show were set aside in a Soldiers Homecoming Fund, to give the boys in service a celebration when they returned in victory. Parts of the play were updated to reflect the current times, including ‘Sally Rand,” “Kate Smith.” “Sophie Tucker,” Eleanor Roosevelt,” “Shirley Temple,” “Carmen Miranda,” “Gypsy Rose Lee” and other well-known celebrities as well as the essential bride and groom. It was difficult to tell if the cast or the audience had more fun; Edward Leiter, the ring bearer, carried a ring of Rieder and Schilling’s best bologna on a soft cushion.

Beginning in 1888, Delano residents crowded the village hall to be entertained by traveling theatricals and home talent plays.

In 1971 the old meeting room above the city offices was once again the center of local theatrical farce. That summer the melodrama “Deadwood Dick” was presented, sponsored by the Delano Recreation Department.
It was complete with olios, house rules and a backdrop of hometown advertising.
Directors were Bill and Sandy Horeis.
Presented three days, August 20-22, Sunday’s standing room only audience included Senator Hubert Humphrey.

The Delano Community Education play in 1988 was “Fools,” featuring Becky Iverson, Tina Gray, Brian Delger, Mark Lewis, Dennis Johnston, Chris Koch, Jim Schmidt, Kathy Hegna, Jackie Johnston, and Ken Schiller.

Barb Roy directed the Delano Community Theater production of M*A*S*H in 1989. Some of the cast members were Rick Workman as Father Mulcahy, Al Holimotz as Klinger, Jim Schmidt as Hawkeye, Scott Shoutz as Trapper John, Dennis Johnston as Col. Blake, Dale Weiman as Radar, Becky Iverson as Hot Lips, and Ken Schiller as Duke Forrest.
Jason Schmidt, Becky Iverson, Jim Schmidt, Ken Schiller, and Melissa Windsperger.
Current dramatic group is the Delano Dramatic Company
Delano Community Bands
Delano has always had interest in having a community band. As early as the summer of 1872, a subscription of $50.00 made possible the organization of the “Delano Cornet Band.”
Delano Cornet Band, date unknown

References to the band were made in the Delano Eagle from then through the next several decades.

*In 1874, the Delano Eagle reported that “in the evening, the band having returned from Buffalo, a lively and happy dance was kept up in Lucas Hall until the witching hour of twelve marked the closing of the Nation’s anniversary.”

*The band went to Charles Eppel’s house to celebrate his 55th birthday in 1891: “The Delano Cornet Band was present in uniform and gave the host the first hint of what was going on by striking up a lively air in front of the house.”

*Prof. R. M. Bohn (also a local barber) retired in 1893 from directing the band for several years He was presented a special plaque by the members of the Cornet band in appreciation for his work.
Fourth of July parade, Railroad Avenue in Delano, ca. 1896. “The parade was led by the Delano Cornet Band in their immaculately new white uniforms.”

The band took part in parades, gave concerts, and traveled to other communities to perform.

*In 1896 the Delano Cornet Band was engaged to attend the first celebration of Holy Mass by Rev. Otto Zachman at St. Michael’s church.

But apparently, the band was not always organized. An article in 1908 Eagle stated that Delano needs “a good band, the material is here but only lacking organization.”

In 1921, C.G. Roosen reminisced that “the Delano Cornet Band was a large asset in the social life of the village for many years and with all the good organizations in that line which we have had since – there has never been one better.”

In 1912 the band was called the Delano Military Band. It played at the ground-breaking for the new St. Peter’s Church, and for its dedication in 1913.

Standing: Charles Carlson, Charles Lohmiller, Frank Yantes, Simon Loch, Sam Ash, Chester Orrison, Carl Weddele, Matt Bernick, Jack Lohmiller

Seated: Herbert Probst, Charles Wood, Pete Peterson, Oscar Hildebrandt, Prof. Beck, Frank Schaffer, C. T. Buckley, Rastey Yantes.
Conductor Professor John Beck

There was a bandstand on Railroad Avenue for concerts, that was later moved to Central Park.

The Delano Military Band gave a concert in the new bandstand on August 5, 1915, and every two weeks thereafter.
Unknown name or date or this band in the bandstand.

This is the Delano Band in the late 1920’s, under the leadership of Alvin Weihe. This group played at surrounding towns, and at all the picnics, parades, and celebrations. They also played a day at the State Fair. The band practiced upstairs in the city hall every Monday evening. Alvin Weihe is standing behind the bass drum in the right.

The community band also occasionally played at the local baseball games. During the 1928 tournament the Delano band furnished music during the morning and afternoon games, as noted by the Delano Eagle.

The current Delano Community Band is an inter-generational, all-volunteer concert band. Established in November 2017, band membership has comprised of musicians ranging from strong high school students to those who’ve been performing for over 50 years. This diversity of experience enables the band to offer growth as well as performance opportunities for area musicians. They rehearse for about 90 minutes on Thursday evenings at 7:00p.m. in the Delano High School band room. Their repertoire spans virtually every major genre of western music from traditional concert band fare to renditions of early music, to adaptations of orchestral pieces, to contemporary iterations of popular music and modern works for band.

stops.title: Lebovsky Building
stops.summary: The Lebovsky Building at 141 Bridge Avenue E. has been part of Delano’s commercial history since at least 1894, when Olof Peterson operated a boot and shoe store there. Over the following decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including the Columbia Clothing Store, shoe and clothing stores operated by the Berlin family and others, a Marshall-Wells associate store, and William Heinen’s hardware business. In 1940, Lebovsky’s Store , a family business founded by Thomas S. Lebovsky on River Street in 1906, moved to the Bridge Street location. The Lebovsky family continued the store for more than four decades, making it a familiar fixture in downtown Delano until it closed in 1984. Since then, the building has been home to Calico Cat Fabrics, the Crow River News, Dwayne’s Games, and Bridge Avenue Ceramics. In 1994, Joe McDonald moved his photography business into the building, beginning another long chapter in the history of this enduring downtown storefront.

body.html: The Lebovsky Building at 141 Bridge Avenue E. has been part of Delano’s commercial history since at least 1894, when Olof Peterson operated a boot and shoe store there. Over the following decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including the Columbia Clothing Store, shoe and clothing stores operated by the Berlin family and others, a Marshall-Wells associate store, and William Heinen’s hardware business. In 1940, Lebovsky’s Store, a family business founded by Thomas S. Lebovsky on River Street in 1906, moved to the Bridge Street location. The Lebovsky family continued the store for more than four decades, making it a familiar fixture in downtown Delano until it closed in 1984. Since then, the building has been home to Calico Cat Fabrics, the Crow River News, Dwayne’s Games, and Bridge Avenue Ceramics. In 1994, Joe McDonald moved his photography business into the building, beginning another long chapter in the history of this enduring downtown storefront.

The building at 141 Bridge Ave. can be traced back a far as 1894, and perhaps even earlier. In 1894 it was a boot and shoe store, owned by Olof Peterson.

In 1905 Mr. Peterson, in conjunction with Louis and Henry Bock and John Stein built the Brick Block Building on Bridge, adjacent to his shoe store. Ole moved next door and occupied his new store. The Delano Eagle reported that his former building was rented by to the Schmidt Bros., of Belle Plain, who bought and shipped poultry, butter, and eggs.

In 1909 Ole Peterson put an addition on his old store and raised the ceiling.
The Columbia Clothing Store was in the building ca. 1913.

It seems likely that Ole Peterson sold his business and buildings to John Berlin, who was also in the shoe business.

In 1919 John Berlin tore out the west wall of his former shoe store and connected the building to his present adjoining store. In December of that same year, O.C. Damsberg opened his Clothing & Gents Furnishing Emporium in the Berlin Building. Damsberg was a tailor, and became known as “Curley the Tailor”
Jasper Berlin, son of John, opened a shoe store in the old stand in 1922. He sold out to Homer F. Ehle in 1926. Ehle had a bankruptcy sale at the end of the year.

In 1936 Robert Gamble opened a new store in the building across from the Delano City Hall, a M.W. Associate Store. The Marshall-Wells Store remained there until 1939.

William Heinen moved his hardware store into the east end of the Brick Block, Ole Petersen’s space, in 1933. It was connected to the building adjoining to the east.

In 1940 Lebovsky’s moved from their store on River Street to their new location on Bridge Street in the Heinen building, across from City Hall.
Inside Lebvosky’s Store

Lebovsky’s original store was built and opened on River Street in 1906 by Thomas S. Lebovsky. When Thomas passed away in 1932, his wife, Mary, continued the business, with the assistance of her son Richard and daughter Ruth. The store was taken over in 1942 by sons Frank and Richard. Richard came from Minneapolis, and Richard recently returned from the service. Frank and his wife Winnifred worked at the family store between 1944 and 1955. Richard and his wife, Madeline “Maggie” Alger, then continued as the proprietors the Lebovsky Store.
Bridge Street, 1970’s Lebovsky’s on the left side.

Lebovsky’s Store closed in 1984 and was sold to Lola Pool, who opened

the Calico Cat Fabrics Store with her co-owner Shirley Krueger.

In 1989 the Crow River News office was in the building, followed by Dwayne’s Games, and from 1991-1993 it was Bridge Avenue Ceramics

Joe McDonald moved into the building in 1994, and it has been the McDonald Photography Studio since then.

stops.title: Longosh Building
stops.subtitle: Built in 1906
stops.summary: Built in 1904 by bricklayer and stonemason John Longosh, the Longosh Building has been part of Delano’s Bridge Avenue streetscape for more than 120 years. Longosh, a German immigrant who arrived in Delano in the 1870s, constructed the two-story brick building with commercial space below and living quarters above. The Longosh Building SoCT Over the decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including a saloon, barber shop, Curley’s clothing store, a harness and leather shop, and Bill’s Shoe Repair. The Longosh Building SoCT Its long history reflects the changing businesses and everyday life of downtown Delano. Today, in 2026, the historic building continues its commercial role as the home of Vintage on Bridge and the Book Nook .

Longosh, a German immigrant who arrived in Delano in the 1870s, constructed the two-story brick building with commercial space below and living quarters above. The Longosh Building SoCT Over the decades, the building housed an assortment of businesses, including a saloon, barber shop, Curley’s clothing store, a harness and leather shop, and Bill’s Shoe Repair. The Longosh Building SoCT Its long history reflects the changing businesses and everyday life of downtown Delano. Today, in 2026, the historic building continues its commercial role as the home of Vintage on Bridge and the Book Nook.

John Longosh was born in Upper Silesia, Germany in 1848, emigrated to the United States in 1872, coming directly to St. Paul, and then came to Delano about a year later. He was by trade a bricklayer and stonemason and built more than one building in Delano.

May 1904 - “John Longosh is getting the material on the ground for the erection of a solid brick building, 24x40, which he will build on his lot on the south side of Bridge Street. It will be a two-story structure, the first floor fitted up for a store and the second floor fixed for living rooms.”

April 9, 1908 – “John Longosh is tearing down his old frame building on Bridge Street and will erect in its place a solid brick structure, 22 x 40.” (on the north side of Bridge Street)

Nov. 4, 1909 – M. P. Berneck is now nicely settled in his new quarters in the John Longosh building on Bridge Street.”
The Longosh building, next to the State Bank of Delano.

1933 - “The Longosh building next to the State Bank of Delano is being renovated and painted and will be the future home of Curley’s Men’s Furnishing store. Curley told the editor he expected to be nicely settled in his new location by the end of next week.”

May 4, 1933 – Curley the Tailor moved next door to the State Bank of Delano.

1936 – “In the fall of 1936 Dr. Guilfoile came to Delano and established his medical practice with offices over what was then Carl Eckman’s barber shop, (Bill’s Shoe Repair in 1979).”

Oct. 7, 1937 – Curley’s and Peters Change Locations.

“Beginning Monday Curley’s clothing store will be located in the building now occupied by Peter’s harness shop, and the harness shop will move into Curley’s present location. Mr. Peter’s bought the building now occupied by Eckman’s barber shop, Dr. Guilfoile, and Curley some time ago. He has made his living quarters above the clothing store and will now move his business over there also. In order that all his customers get quickly acquainted with his new location Bud Dainsberg is advertising a weeklong sale to be held in his new location starting Monday.”
Mr. Peter’s sold his harness and leather shop to Claus and Lillian Eckhoff. In about 1942.

The business was bought by Bill Benson in 1973, who had Bill’s Shoe Repair.

The Longosh building on the south side of Bridge Avenue has been a saloon, a barbershop, a clothing store, a harness and leather shop, and a shoe repair shop. Today, in 2026, it is the home of Vintage on Bridge and the Book Nook.

stops.title: State Bank of Delano Building
stops.subtitle: Built 1908
stops.summary: 1908: The State Bank of Delano was incorporated. 1910: The State Bank of Delano and the Wright County Bank was consolidated.

body.html:
• 1908: The State Bank of Delano was incorporated.

  • 1910: The State Bank of Delano and the Wright County Bank was consolidated.

Interior view of State Bank Delano on Bridge Avenue circa 1912. Seated behind the desk is Charles McDonald and standing is Louis Probst. The customer is Reverend Hilding Eagle. The First bank president was Henry C. Bull.

1908: State Bank of Delano with white enamel brick front. The main banking room had a tile floor, an Italian marble wainscoting, with verde-antique base and rail. The fixtures were the best quarter sawed oak, with oxidized copper grillwork and every convenience for the conduct of business. The vault door was a massive Victor and gave a finish to the counting room, which was most striking. With its steel ceiling and walls was insured cleanliness, to say nothing of the pleasing effect. But decoration alone were not sought, the bank being supplied with a Victor safe which made losses by burglary impossible. Hot water was used for heating and electricity or lighting. The interior equipment was undoubtedly the most artistic and best in point of quality of any bank of its size in the state. In addition to general banking business this house wrote insurance in many of the vest companies and handled real estate. (as described The Great Northwest Magazine, December 1909).
State Bank of Delano circa 1915

• 1975: The State Bank of Delano moved to a new location on Railroad Ave (now the Delano Great Rivers Public Library).

  • 1988: The building was occupied by Flowers by Styve

  • 2000: The building was occupied by Bridge Floral

  • 2002: The State Bank of Delano moved to a new location on Highway 12

  • The building has been faithfully restored by the office of MacLean Law Office.
The old bank vault is now 'the most secure bathroom in Delano'.

stops.title: West Brick Block on Bridge
stops.subtitle: Built 1905
stops.summary: The west end of Delano’s Brick Block has been home to a remarkable variety of businesses and community services since the building was constructed in 1905. J. L. Stein developed this portion of the block on the site of an old blacksmith shop, with the Northwestern Telephone Company occupying rooms upstairs soon afterward. Over the following decades, the building housed a men’s clothing store, the Delano Variety Store, a furniture business, the Comet Theater, and Dr. F. R. Shanahan’s dental practice. By the 1930s it was home to the Boyce Funeral Home, and in 1941 Jack Schumacher purchased the property, remodeled the storefront, and moved his Jack Sprat grocery store there. The business later became Jack’s Food Guild , remaining until Schumacher’s retirement in the mid-1970s. The space eventually became part of Coast to Coast Hardware and today forms part of the Jerome Event Center , continuing the Brick Block’s long role in Delano’s downtown commercial life.

Over the following decades, the building housed a men’s clothing store, the Delano Variety Store, a furniture business, the Comet Theater, and Dr. F. R. Shanahan’s dental practice. The business later became Jack’s Food Guild, remaining until Schumacher’s retirement in the mid-1970s. The space eventually became part of Coast to Coast Hardware and today forms part of the Jerome Event Center, continuing the Brick Block’s long role in Delano’s downtown commercial life.

In February of 1905 it was announced that a solid brick block would be built on Bridge Street by Olof Peterson, Henry and Louis Bock, and J. L. Stein. J.L. Stein purchased the lot cornering on the alley and Bridge Street, where a blacksmith shop stood for years, and had the old landmark torn down to make room for his new block. The building was completed in 8 months. J.L. Stein’s was the west 25 x 90 bend of the building.

The Northwestern Telephone Co. decided to locate in the rooms above Stein’s new building in June of 1906; the erection of the brick block had just completed when John L. Stein died in October of 1906.

Leo J. Plattner opened a Gents Furnishing and Clothing Store in the Stein building in 1907, sold out in 1909, when Holmberg & Co. rented it. Later that year Bernard Blomquist opened the Delano Variety Store in Mrs. Stein’s building. Blomquist changed to being a furniture dealer, but remained in that location until 1915, when the Comet Theater moved into the west end of the brick block.

Dr. F. R. Shanahan, dentist, opened a dental parlor in the old Commercial Club rooms in the Brick Block in 1919, and he and his wife moved into one of Mrs. Stein’s apartments in the Brick Block in 1921.

Mrs. J. L. Stein died in 1939. The Boyce Funeral Home was in the building in the 1930’s, moving out when Jack Schumacher bought the building from the Stein Estate in 1941. He put on a new front, featuring large display windows, and moved his Jack Sprat grocery store from around the corner. The store became a Food Guild Store in 1951, known as Jack’s Food Guild. Jack retired in the mid 1970’s.

This is a photo taken in the late 1970’s. There is no sign on the west end of the brick block. The space eventually became part of the Coast to Coast Hardware store, and today is part of the Jerome Event Center.

stops.title: Beauty Shops
stops.summary: Delano’s beauty shops emerged in the late 1920s as changing fashions, especially women “bobbing” their hair, created a new demand for professional hairstyling. Martha Lindsley advertised a beauty shop in her home in 1926, and by the 1930s more Delano women were independently owning and operating their own shops. Over the decades, businesses such as the Mella-Dor Beauty Box, Kitty’s Beauty Shop, the Bridge Corner Barber and Beauty Shop, and others became fixtures of the community. Margaret “Kitty” Kittock’s business survived the 1971 Delano Theater fire and eventually became the Downtown Beauty Shop, which Pat Schroeder operated until her retirement in 2025. Together, these shops and the women who operated them reflect nearly a century of changing hairstyles, entrepreneurship, and small-town life in Delano.

Although there were barber shops in Delano almost from the beginning of the village, beauty shops for women did not appear until the late 1920’s, when women began cutting or “bobbing” their hair. The first ads in the Delano Eagle were from Armand Stein’s barber shop, in 1926.

That same year Martha Lindsley advertised Martha’s Beauty Shop, located in her home on 3rd Street.

The Lindsley Family Barber Shop was advertised in 1927 on River Street, and in 1929 it was called Lindsley’s Barber Shop and Mertha’s Beauty Shop, Mr. and Mrs. M. G. Lindsley, proprietors.

More women began to individually own and operate beauty shops in Delano. In the 1930’s.

Angie’s Beauty Shoppe was in the Brick Block Building in 1941, but 1943 it became the Mella-Dor Beauty Box. The name of the shop was a combination of the end of Armella Simm’s first name, and the beginning of Dorothy Westmark’s first name, the proprietors.

The Bock Brothers moved their barber shop to the building on the corner of Bridge and River Street in 1907. By the 1930’s Edward Bock and his wife Luverne were operating the Bridge Corner Barber and Beauty Shop. They sold to Leslie and Rose Krumm in 1941.

Rose was a graduate of the Brady-Rogers Beauty School in Minneapolis. Expert hair styling to suit the individual won Mrs. Krumm a large following from Delano and the surrounding area.

Adeline’s Beauty Shop opened in the same location in 1948.
Sharon (Hanseman) Gonsior advertised Sharon’s Beauty Shop in the 1957.

Margaret Kittock purchased the shop in 1946, and in 1948 moved it next to Armand’s Barber Shop on River Street.

When the Delano Theater burned in 1971, Kitty’s Beauty Shop was in the building, and destroyed.

A few months later Kitty announced that she would be reopening in the former furniture building
Pat Schroeder began working for Kitty in 1984 and took over the shop in 1989. Known for years as the Downtown Beauty Shop, Pat remained in business here until she retired in 2025.
Many beauticians have served the community over the years. Doreen Schrode, Sue Gallus and many others.

stops.title: Big Wood Garden Club
stops.subtitle: EST. 2002
stops.summary: Founded in 2002 as part of the Delano Dream Team’s effort to beautify Historic Downtown Delano, the Big Woods Garden Club brought together people who shared a love of gardening and a desire to improve their community. Through plant sales, garden tours, educational programs, and countless hours of volunteer work, members created and maintained community gardens, landscaped the Delano Public Library, supported local organizations, cared for area roadsides, and helped beautify downtown Delano. When River Front Park was established following the installation of the downtown flood walls in 2017, the club once again contributed both plants and helping hands to beautify River Street. They have recently established garden to accent some of the sculptures installed in the Delano Sculpture Park. Over the years, the Big Woods Garden Club combined community service, gardening education, friendship, and plenty of “green thumbs” to leave a lasting mark on Delano and the surrounding area.

The first executive board included: 

President - Peggy Zimmerman-Belbeck

Vice President - Debbie De Beer

Secretary - Bridgette Scheppat

Treasurer - Judy Vanderlinde

Members at large:  Jackie Singer, Betty Rieder and June Sutton

The members met once a month.  Each meeting had a educational speaker, demonstration or a tour, and often a new members.

​The Big Woods Garden Club is dedicated to providing a variety of gardening related programs including: education of club members; planning, installing and assisting in maintaining community plantings for the beautification of park, building and open spaces; raising awareness and funds for community horticultural programs and efforts; and providing a social environment for convening of individuals sincerely interested in and demonstrating a willingness to work and to share their horticultural knowledge with others. The Big Woods Garden Club services the areas of western Hennepin County, Eastern Wright County and northern Carver County of MN.

First Plant Sale was held May 17th, 2003 to provide funds for a their first community project, a flower garden on River Street north of Bridge along the fence on the river bank.  The site had 3 buildings on it that house many business over the years but all were gone, leaving an area perfect for a garden.

National Honors Society, and club members and their husbands helped in the two day project of clearing sod, prepping the soil, planting the garden and mulching.  Trees and shrubs were purchase from the plant sale proceeds and  members and the community donated plants.

Dream Team Adopt-a -Pot - encouraged businesses and individuals to plant and maintain one of the large planters downtown.  The planters were judged by Master Gardener Club members and continued the tradition for many years.
In 2004 the Garden Club landscaped the new Delano Public Library
The Club adopted a section of County Road 6 from 2003-16. In 2016 the club has adopted County Road 30 and picks up any debris in the spring and fall.
When the flood walls were installed in 2017 and the River Front Park was established the Big Woods Garden Club donated money for the plants and “women” power to the area once more.
In recent years the Garden Club has established and maintained the gardens around the permanent sculptures in the Delano Sculpture Park.

‘Project Redefined ‘Garden

‘Flood of ‘65” Garden

Big Woods Garden Club Annual Dinner has become a tradition as the gardening season winds down. Every year there is an informative guest speaker and is held in a local restaurant.

Over the years the club provided gardening education through expert speakers, workshops and tours.  The group has helped beautify a number of areas in the community and has provided many social hours with like minded people with green thumbs.

The Big Woods Garden Club began in 2002 as part the Delano Dream Team’s initiative to beautify Historic Downtown Delano.  Debbie DeBeer the chairperson of the Dream Dream contacted Jackie Singer, Wright County Master Gardener, to ask if there were any garden clubs  that could help. Jackie recommended Peggy Zimmerman-Belbeck, a Master Gardener Intern to take on creating a garden club as her intern project for the task. They invited community members with an interest in gardening to join the first meeting was July 25, 2002, held at Steinmetz Realty.

stops.title: Cramer Building
stops.summary: The Cramer Building at 224 River Street N. has been part of Delano’s commercial history since the late 1800s and was long associated with one of the city’s oldest meat markets. Joseph Cramer operated a meat market on River Street as early as 1879, later joined by his son Frank, and by the mid-1880s Cramer was constructing a new brick building at the site. The meat market tradition continued under J. M. Wandok and later Everett LaFave, whose market remained a familiar River Street business for decades. In 1972, nearly a century after Cramer began his business, the building became home to Delano TV and subsequently housed a variety of businesses. Today, the historic storefront is home to LuLu’s Retail Therapy , which opened in January 2020 and offers women’s clothing and accessories, baby items, home décor, and gifts.

The history of the building at 224 River Street goes back a long way, and that history also is the narrative of one of the oldest meat markets in Delano.

Joseph Cramer was the proprietor of a meat market below the bridge on River street as early as 1879. The 1880 census lists Joseph as a butcher and the owner of a meat market, with his son Frank working with him as a butcher. Both were still there in 1885, when the Delano Eagle reported that Joseph Cramer was taking the lead in a building boom on River street, and “soon would have a fine new (brick) block.”
Oct. 2, 1879 newspaper ad
A 1894 map of Delano shows a brick building, a meat market, at this location.
In 1893 an article in the Delano Eagle described F. A. Cramer as being “the successor to the oldest meat market in the city.”
F. A. Cramer’s Meat Market, 1897

In 1903 J. M. Wandok purchased the building from Mrs. Joseph (Augusta) Cramer. Wandok was already occupying it as a meat market at that time. Wandok built the brick building just to the south of his shop in 1908; it became a bank, and then the post office. Wandok had retired by 1920 according to the census records. Louis A. Kuehn was working as a butcher in 1922 and is enumerated on the 1930 census as a butcher in Delano.
April 9, 1906 newspaper ad
In 1936 Everett LaFave opened his butcher shop in Delano; he had been working there as a meat cutter in Delano since 1933.
LaFave’s Meat Market

The Mainstreet, a special edition of the Delano Eagle published in 1946, described LaFave’s Meat Market as being next to the post office. Everett LaFave continued working as a butcher into the 1960’s.

In 1972 Jeff Merriman opened the new Delano TV store in the LaFave building on River street, nearly 100 years after Joseph Cramer first opened his meat market. During the following years a number of different businesses occupied the building.

The building became the home of LuLu’s Retail Therapy, opened by Laurie Schaust in January, 2020. Lulus specializes in women's clothes and accessories, and also sells baby items, home decor and gift items.

stops.title: Delano Chamber of Commerce
stops.subtitle: EST. 1967
stops.summary: The Delano Area Chamber of Commerce traces its beginnings to 1939, when local businessmen organized a Santa Claus Day for Delano children, an effort that grew into a broader movement to promote the community and support local commerce. On June 3, 1941, the group formally organized as a Civic Club dedicated to advancing the interests of local merchants, expanding Delano’s trade area, and encouraging community activities and improvements. In 1953, Articles of Incorporation were adopted and the organization became the Delano Civic and Commerce Club . Through community celebrations, banquets, promotions, and other civic projects, the organization played an important role in bringing Delano’s business community together and supporting the growth and vitality of the city.

body.html: The Delano Area Chamber of Commerce traces its beginnings to 1939, when local businessmen organized a Santa Claus Day for Delano children, an effort that grew into a broader movement to promote the community and support local commerce. On June 3, 1941, the group formally organized as a Civic Club dedicated to advancing the interests of local merchants, expanding Delano’s trade area, and encouraging community activities and improvements. In 1953, Articles of Incorporation were adopted and the organization became the Delano Civic and Commerce Club. Through community celebrations, banquets, promotions, and other civic projects, the organization played an important role in bringing Delano’s business community together and supporting the growth and vitality of the city.

The start of the Chamber started back in fall of 1939, when Don Bartlett and Bob McEachren started a movement to hold a Santa Claus Day for children in Delano and the surrounding trade area. They worked with Cliff Lundsten, and Delano merchants funded 600 bags of candy and fruit for children at that first event.

In fall 1940, the effort grew. A committee headed by Ed Dalheimer, Sham Jaunich, Jack Tomnitz and John F. Tischler, with help from the American Legion Auxiliary, prepared 1,000 treat bags. Again, local businesspeople paid for the event.

The important date for the Chamber's organizational history is June 3, 1941. A meeting was called specifically to form a Civic Club whose purpose was to advance the business interests of local merchants and expand Delano's trade area through promotions, community activities and improvements.

First Officers

Chairman - Carl Hanseman

Vice Chairman - Jack Schumacher

Secretary - Harold Henk

Treasurer - Harry Kuka

The club's first dinner meeting was June 17, 1941, at the Last Roundup, with 60 business and civic-minded people attending. Three committees were immediately established: Resolutions, Membership and Entertainment.

A second milestone occurred on April 8, 1953, when Articles of Incorporation were drawn up and the organization formally took the name:

“The Delano Civic and Commerce Club.”

Its officers at that time were:

President - Harry Kuka

1st Vice President - Bill Wallisch

2nd Vice President - C.N. Lundsten

Secretary & Treasurer - Al Weihe

The historical account says the organization sponsored the Annual Athletic Banquet for many years and continued the Christmas party that had begun around 1940. It also produced a Community Calendar that was distributed to area residents, with the programs financed by club members.

There is independent evidence connecting this organization to today's Chamber. An obituary for longtime Delano businessman Carroll J. Lundeen, who opened Lundeen's Men's Store in Delano in 1953, describes him as a member of the Civic Club and explicitly calls that club “a forerunner of the Delano Chamber of Commerce.”

According the Office of the Minnesota Secretary of State on November 23,1954 filed as a nonprofit corporation for Delano Civic and Commerce Club.

From the 1960’s to 1990’s the Delano Civic and Commerce Club hosted many long-standing events like Christmas/ Santa Claus Day, Annual Athletic Banquet and Community Calendar that was sponsored and paid for by the members of Delano Civic and Commerce Club.

On October 20, 1993, Delano Civic and Commerce Club changed its name to Delano Area Chamber of Commerce.

From the beginning Delano Civic and Commerce Club and now the Delano Area Chamber of Commerce have hosted events, committees and supporting local businesses. The events, committees and businesses have changed over the years. The focus has always been ‘equipping members to thrive in our business community’.

To find out more about Delano Area Chamber of Commerce is doing now, visit their website at www.delanochamber.com

stops.title: Delano Granite Works
stops.subtitle: Founded 1917
stops.summary: Founded in 1917 by Bert Gilmer , Delano Granite Works grew from a small monument shop into an internationally significant Delano industry and, by 1944, the world’s largest granite memorial retailer . From its plant along the Crow River, the company expanded dramatically, owning quarries, production facilities, and a sales organization while adopting increasingly sophisticated equipment for cutting, polishing, and finishing stone. It became one of Delano’s largest employers and an important part of the community’s civic and economic life. In 1964, the company expanded beyond monuments into structural granite, supplying stone for projects including the General Mills headquarters . Don Gilmer succeeded his father in leading the company in 1956, and the Granite Works continued operating until its closure in 1984 . Although the former industrial site has since been redeveloped, granite found throughout Delano remains a visible reminder of a company that helped shape the community for nearly seven decades.

It became one of Delano’s largest employers and an important part of the community’s civic and economic life. In 1964, the company expanded beyond monuments into structural granite, supplying stone for projects including the General Mills headquarters. Don Gilmer succeeded his father in leading the company in 1956, and the Granite Works continued operating until its closure in 1984. Although the former industrial site has since been redeveloped, granite found throughout Delano remains a visible reminder of a company that helped shape the community for nearly seven decades.

Delano’s first nationally recognized manufacturer was the world’s largest granite memorial retailer by 1944. They also expanded into granite exteriors for construction. The Delano Granite Works owned their own quarries, production facilities, and sales organization. What once was done almost entirely by hand evolved to the use of diamond and wire saws, machines for polishing, and flame burners for thermal texturing. During its time, it was the area’s largest employer, promoting and modeling civic involvement. The granite around Delano is a reminder of this legacy.
First being located in various places on River Street and ...
… Bridge Avenue in the early years.

Bert Gilmer, at 23 was a young newly wed salesman in 1917, opened a small monument shop, hiring a man to do the cutting, while he went door-to-door selling memorials. That business grew to be the biggest retailer of monuments in the world.
In 1927, Bert Gilmer built a new plant along the Crow River’s edge, off of River Street behind the house they lived in.
1927 Aerial view of Delano Granite Works Bert Gilmer’s home is shown to the right of center.

~1930’s. Bert Gilmer's first expansion of his new plant added 2,000 sq. ft. of production space with newer granite cutting and polishing equipment, plus an enlarged office building to accommodate his rapidly growing monument business.
President Harry Truman writes thank you for Delano Granite Works created monument!

In 1953 the last major expansion of the Monumental Division with the addition of 50,000 sq.ft. of all glassed-in production space. (Energy conservation wasn’t an issue in those days). This expansion included a large, new state-of-the-art slab polishing line, multiple wire saws, and expanded sand-blast lettering department. Bert Gilmer’s home was converted to office and meeting space when he moved to Minneapolis.
Don Gilmer took over the business in 1956.
Their outdoor billboard advertising slogan was….
“Drive Carefully – We Can Wait.”
"Ferdinand the Bull", Don Gilmer's Office on Wheels

~ 1963. With the expansion into the Structural Granite Division, additional wire-sawing capability was added to the Monumental Division. This included constructing the wire “pully” system housed in the tower and cupola (upper left).
Stone Cutters at Work
1964 Delano Granite Works started making structural granite for building purposes.
Delano Granite Works siding on the General Mills Headquarters

1965. (Aerial view) The last major building expansion. The new 25,000 sq. ft. “Butler Building” located to the far northwest end of the building was added to house the growing Structural Granite Division with new large format sawing and polishing equipment, "flame-texturing" system, plus added wire saws for cutting thin slabs and curved slabs.
In 1972, the tower was encased with a facade of polished Dakota Mahogany granite when new owner Rembrandt Enterprises converted the front of the production plant into new office spaces.
Delano Rembrandt Building
In 1984 the Granite Works was closed.
The buildings house a number of smaller businesses and companies, including Kirby Vacuums and Electrical and Appliance Recycling.
In 2022 the building were demolished and the Granite Works Apartment complex was built.

stops.title: Delano United Diversity Task Force
stops.subtitle: Founded in 2017
stops.summary: Founded in 2017 as Delano United , the Delano United Diversity Task Force (DUDTF) is a grassroots volunteer organization working to make the Delano area a more welcoming and equitable community. Its efforts have included community speakers and book discussions, support for student and parent groups, anti-bullying and equity initiatives, participation in local parades, the weekly On Welcoming newspaper column, and advocacy for affordable housing. More recently, the group has helped research and share the area’s Indigenous history as part of Delano’s Sesquicentennial activities, including contributing information for the commemorative book and connecting the mural project with Dakota cultural resources. Today, DUDTF continues to partner with local organizations and encourage volunteers to help foster inclusion and a sense of welcome for everyone who lives, works, plays, and prays in the Delano community.

Its efforts have included community speakers and book discussions, support for student and parent groups, anti-bullying and equity initiatives, participation in local parades, the weekly On Welcoming newspaper column, and advocacy for affordable housing. More recently, the group has helped research and share the area’s Indigenous history as part of Delano’s Sesquicentennial activities, including contributing information for the commemorative book and connecting the mural project with Dakota cultural resources. Today, DUDTF continues to partner with local organizations and encourage volunteers to help foster inclusion and a sense of welcome for everyone who lives, works, plays, and prays in the Delano community.

The Delano United Diversity Task Force (DUDTF), which began as Delano United in the spring of 2017, is a grassroots group of Delano area folks whose mission is to make Delano a more welcoming and equitable community. Activities of the group have included bringing diversity-related speakers to town, coordinating book discussions, supporting the high school’s LGBTQ group, supporting a parents’ group working to address tolerance, equity, and anti-bullying efforts, participating in two 4th of July parades, writing a weekly column (On Welcoming) for the Delano Herald Journal, coordinating with the Sesquicentennial Committee to raise awareness of the Delano area’s Indigenous history, and advocating for affordable housing.

City administrator, Phil Kern, was cited in the Delano Herald Journal, May 1, 2017… “(Delano United) was formed when representatives from the city, school district, clergy, Chamber of Commerce, and community groups got together to do something to make a statement…We want to see a grassroots effort. We want to see a lot of people get involved in this and not just be six to eight people sitting in a conference room trying to determine what happens.”

In the summer of 2017, the Mpls. Star Tribune featured Delano in its quarterly Sunday magazine. The U.S. Dept. of Justice recognized the DUDTF and sent reps to town (twice) to support the formation of the group’s organizational structure.

The feature article, “Delano: The town saying no to hate… An act of racism stunned Delano. Now residents are fighting for a better future – for all” was written by John Reinan and published in the Mpls Star Tribune in June of 2017. https://www.startribune.com/delano-the-town-saying-no-to-hate/431034233
Candle Light Vigil
Community Organizational Meeting
4th of July Parade

During 2025, a subcommittee of the DUDTF researched the Delano area’s pre-settlement history and supported Marcia Brakke as she developed the chapter in Delano’s Sesquicentennial book about the Indigenous background of Minnesota. In addition, we shared Indigenous information with Leanne Wurzer, the artist of the mural, connecting her to Hoċokata Ṫi, the Dakota cultural center in Shakopee. https://shakopeedakota.org/culture-history/hocokata-ti-cultural-center/

We also offered Indigenous-related suggestions to Nick Neaton for Senior Center field trips. In our “On Welcoming” column, we highlighted past and present experiences of Indigenous people.

The DUDTF continues to look for ways to partner with local groups and spread the message of inclusion and a sense of welcome for Delano area citizens and newcomers. It's a community volunteer group, and future events depend on volunteers to make them happen.

The closing of each On Welcoming column reads, If you are interested in helping make Delano a more welcoming community for all who want to live, work, play, and pray here, please contact the Delano United Diversity Task Force by email at delanouniteddiversity@gmail.com. You can also find us on Facebook: “Delano United – Diversity” where you’ll find our weekly newspaper columns.

stops.title: First National Bank of Delano
stops.subtitle: Built 1908
stops.summary: Built in late 1908 to house the Wright County Bank, the building at 220 River Street North has been a familiar part of downtown Delano for more than a century. By 1910, the bank was settled into its impressive new quarters, which featured oak interior finishes, tile floors, a steel ceiling, electric lighting, and other modern conveniences. The building later became home to First National Bank and, beginning in March 1965, the Delano Post Office. Over the years it has continued to serve the community through a variety of businesses, including a real estate office and photography studio, reflecting the many changes that have shaped Delano’s downtown.

The building later became home to First National Bank and, beginning in March 1965, the Delano Post Office. Over the years it has continued to serve the community through a variety of businesses, including a real estate office and photography studio, reflecting the many changes that have shaped Delano’s downtown.

This building was built in late 1908 to house the Wright County Bank, which had moved from its location on Railroad Avenue. The Delano Eagle reported in January 1909 that the bank was settled in its new home on River street, and was in possession of “fine, commodious quarters with new fixtures and furnishings throughout.” The interior finish was in oak with a tile floor, steel ceiling and attractive electric fixtures. It was heated with a furnace, insuring comfort, and “the general appearance of the whole a credit to the town.”
In this picture of lower River street from 1910, the Wright County Bank building is fourth from the right, with its white awning extended.
In October of 1910 the Wright County Bank and the State Bank of Delano consolidated, and a new bank, the First National Bank, occupied the building on River Street.

The Delano Post Office moved into the building in 1926.  Here we can see people looking out of the Post Office window at the flood in 1965. The post office moved to their new and current building on the corner of River Street and Railroad Avenue later that same year.
Since that time, the building has been a real estate office, Linda's Photography Studio, and is in 2021 the home of The Realty Lab.

stops.title: GP Schaffer Building
stops.subtitle: Built 1897
stops.summary: Built in 1906, the two-story brick building at 248 River Street North has been part of Delano’s downtown story for more than a century. Originally constructed by E. F. Ziebarth and Thomas Lebovsky, it has housed an ever-changing variety of businesses and residents through the decades, surviving changes in ownership, a major fire, and the evolution of downtown Delano itself. Today, following an extensive renovation, the historic building is known as the Whiskey Jar Pud and Eatery and continues its long tradition as a vibrant part of the community.

Originally George Schaffer opened a store on the corner of River St. and Franklin Ave. in 1888/89.

Then this brick building was built as a general merchandise store by G.P. Schaffer.
The building originally had a front balcony and porch.

The Schaffer building housed Geo. P. Schaffer & Son, a general mercantile business that handled a full line of dry goods, furnishings, boys’ clothing, hats, caps, shoes, groceries, crockery and glassware.

• 1909: The business was know as Geo P Schaffer and Son

  • 1915: Geo P Schaffer's son Franky took over the business1926 the building housed the J.C.N Peterson Mercantile Company

  • 1946: Marvin Schmidt opened the Red & White food store.

  • 1950-Present: The building has housed various retail businesses and survived the 1965 flood.
The rejuvenation of the wall ads on the side of the building was done as an Eagle Scout project by McKay Elwood in 2009.

Graffiti or History???

stops.title: Crow River Floods/Wagon Bridge
stops.summary: The first people to travel the Crow River were the Wahpekute (Shooters Among the Leaves) band of the Oceti Sakowin meaning Seven Council Fires, known as the Great Sioux Nation. In 1853, Wright County was open to white settlement. Trappers, traders, farmers, and shopkeepers began to move into the Big Woods following the Crow River to the area which was to become Delano. body.html:
The first people to travel the Crow River were the Wahpekute (Shooters Among the Leaves) band of the Oceti Sakowin meaning Seven Council Fires, known as the Great Sioux Nation.

In 1853, Wright County was open to white settlement. Trappers, traders, farmers, and shopkeepers began to move into the Big Woods following the Crow River to the area which was to become Delano.

Although the river provided transportation, power and recreation, Delano has had a long history of high water, ice dams and flooding.

The Crow River Bridges provided a important link between settlements on both sides of the river when the water was not low enough to ford.
1868: First wooden bridge was built in Crow River (Delano) by the village, town proprietors and the township.
The first wooden bridge over the Crow River in Delano can be seen in fore front of this photo circa 1868

Borsch’s store was located at the corner of Bridge Avenue and River Street., facing the river. You can see the beginning of the wooden bridge, the first bridge built in Crow River (Delano.)

Built in the village of Delano in 1868, the village paying $150, the town proprietors about the same, and the township the remainder. In 1879 the bridge was entirely rebuilt. In 1882 it was repaired and replanked at a cost of about $230, of which the town paid $100 and the village the remainder.

In 1887 a special election was held to vote on a proposition to rebuild the wooden bridge across the Crow River; the citizens vetoed it by a vote of 23 for and 50 against.

1888 – a special election was held and by a vote of 51 to 49 the proposition of expending $1000 to repair the wooden bridge was again rejected. Another special election was held three weeks later, to consider the matter of spending an amount not exceeding $4000 for an iron bridge. It was rejected by a vote of 85 to 67.

1889 – In April a special election was held to consider the matter of issuing bonds not exceeding $4000 to take up floating debt and to aid in construction of an iron bridge, the bridge not to exceed $2,500. It was rejected by a vote of 71 to 65. Another special election was held in May and by a vote of 115 to 8 it was decided to issue bonds amounting to $3,000 to cover the floating debt. By the end of the year the iron bridge across the Crow River was completed.
The wagon bridge allowed only one vehicle at a time to cross. It also had a pedestrian walkway on one side.

The 1952 flood waters covered all but a few inches of the wagon bridge. A new bridge had been sought by Delano on and off over the next 20 years when in January 1964, the Board of County Commissioners finally authorized its construction. Plans were made to move the wagon bridge a short distance upstream so that it could be used as a footbridge while the new structure was being completed.

Delano’s historic old wagon bridge, which had withstood the battering of many floods, proved to be almost too much for the two giants cranes which moved it to provide a walkway across the river while the new bridge was being constructed. The weight of the bridge, while it was being moved, lifted the cranes four feet off the ground and almost resulted in the bridge being dropped into the river.

Here is the old wagon bridge during the 1965 flood. It was just resting temporarily on piles as the piers for the new bridge were already in place. There was the added concern that the floodwater would wash it away and damage the new piers.

The new bridge was finished following the flood in 1965. It was officially opened on September 24, 1965, with a ribbon cutting ceremony. The celebration included talks by city officials, and visiting dignitaries, a drawing for grand prizes, a square dance exhibition on the new bridge, and finally having the bridge thrown open for public dancing.
The new concrete bridge consists of a 30-foot roadway and two four-feet sidewalks.
In July of 1984, the bridge received a new deck.

The waters of the Crow River continue to go up and down. In 2019 the bridge was closed again in March for a few days because of the high water. The new flood containment system, installed in 2015, can be seen in this photo of the bridge.
Delano Floods

Being a river town, Delano has a long history of high water, ice dams, and flooding. It even had a dam for a short time:

In 1876, George F. Walker, who then owned the steam saw mill and grist mill first erected by Miner Ball and E. D. Barnett in 1869, put a great deal of energy, time and money into the construction of a dam across the river a short distance above the railroad bridge and attempted to run the mill with a turbine, wheel and cable. In April 1877 the ice took part of it away, the land south of town was overflowed and after a long trial, the scheme had to be abandoned. In 1878 the dam itself was abandoned.
The Flood of 1897

1897 When Delano was young the river flowing through it was known as the raging Crow. Since many present day residents can hardly believe the description of the river given by one of the early explorers, “A raging stream flowing between steep, gooseberry bush covered banks,” we present here an early picture of the Crow on the rampage. The picture, sent to us by Adam Horsch, shows the Crow on April 5, 1897. The lumber yard stands on the site of the present power plant. The house pictured is in the same location as the present Oscar Leiter home. The water at the time reached over what today is the state highway, and as can be seen on the wagon wheels was about two feet high at this point. The driver of the wagon was Mr. Cunningham, the Watertown dray man.

(from the Delano Eagle, May 2, 1940)
The Flood of 1916

(from the Delano Eagle, March 30, 1916)

“A number of buildings in the lower part of town, including River Street business houses, are troubled with flooded basements owing to the high stage of water in the river. The river is still rising and the water is higher than for several years. Those who have leisure time find amusement watching the ice go by and speculating on the height to which it will go. The Luce Line bridge at Watertown has been damaged and the old Rockford bridge, we are informed, has been partly swept away.”
This picture was taken at the north end of Delano, near what is now Central Park.
The baseball grandstand is in the background of this picture.

This picture was probably taken from the railroad bridge looking north, as you can see the wagon bridge, St. Joseph’s Church steeple, and the flour mill that stood where the Delano Granite Works later was located.

Again, this picture is probably taken from the railroad bridge. The steeple of the public school is on the left, and the city hall and water tower closer to the right. Several downtown buildings on the riverbank were in the floodwaters.

The Delano Eagle reported that during the high water several motor boats had been using the river, and on Sunday quite a number of young people enjoyed the sensation of gliding along the big stream without the effort of rowing. After the flood reached its peak, and began to subside, several of the low places around the village were still inundated and many cellars had several feet of water in them, concluding how fortunate it was that there had been no heavy rain, or considerable damage would have resulted.
Flood of 1952

From the Delano Eagle, April 10, 1952:

“Crow River Rose To An All Time High on Thursday of this week and at 2:00 o’clock press time the water was till rising. Large sections of the town are under water and 36 families have evacuated their homes. Both the wagon bridge downtown and the highway bridge had their beds awash as this was written. The wagon bridge lacked but a few inches of having the water completely cover it. All the land in the area of the park and extending south as far as Ash Street on Third Street is underwater. The river also overflowed its banks on the south end of town and River Street was flooded for two blocks, as far as Rockford Street. Bridge Street was covered with floodwaters from the power plant to the St. Paul’s Evangelical and Reformed church and part of the street was washed out by the swirling water. Most of Highway 12 from the creamery to Bridge Street was also under water and traffic was being routed around Delano.”

This article was published in the St. Cloud Times (St. Cloud, Minnesota) on April 11:

“The Crow River threatened the power plant and the bridge at Delano, where water is still rising. The power plant has been sandbagged. About three blocks at each end of main street is under water. The main highway bridge is holding back about a foot of water on its upstream side and a downtown bridge is taking a beating, with water just splashing on the floor of the bridge. About 40 families in the Delano area have been forced from their homes.”

Volunteer crews helped Cramers rescue their herd of cattle from their flooded barn and drove them through town to the stockyards.

Volunteers carried calves to safety.

Other farms along the river were also evacuated.
This photo, dated 4-10-52, is the same farm shown in the 1916 flood photo. It was the Helmuth Schauer farm, located at the north end of Central Park.

The 1952 flood set an all-time record mark , and damage ran into thousands of dollars. Only a valiant effort by a crew of volunteers working around the clock saved the power plat from possible destruction. As it was, about $2000 worth of pumps were purchased to help in the fight and much repair work was needed when the waters subsided. The village also ran into considerable expenses repairing streets which were ripped part by the floodwaters, sidewalks that were undermined by the swirling currents, and cleaning up the park which became littered with flotsam.
Flood of 1957

Again, in 1957, high water on the normally placid Crow River brought forecasts that new flood records would be set for much of the length of the lower river. The crest of the 1957 flood reached Delano on June 25, at 15.7 feet, nearly a foot higher that the record set in April 1952. Only trucks and tractors were able to use Highway 12. The Crow River was about 12 feet above its normal level. The Bridge Street bridge connecting Main Street and Highway 12 was threatened. Cars were underwater in parking lots in the business district and sandbags were ineffective in some attempts to keep the Crow away from buildings near the river.

The June 27 Delano Eagle (Delano, Minnesota) proclaimed: Torrential Rains Caused An All-Time Record Flood Here sending the Crow over its banks to inundate almost half of Delano as well a hundreds of acres of farm lands along the course of the stream. The trouble began with intermittent rains during the preceding three weeks, causing the river to raise a couple of feet, but then there came a cloudburst that poured over inches of rain into the area in one afternoon. The river rose rapidly for two days, and soon left its banks in the south end of town and water started coursing through River Street. The north end of town also went under water. The water continued to raise an inch or more an hour, and crews worked around the clock to raise and strengthen sand bag dikes. The crest was reached on the fourth day, from 2 to 6 inches above the record breaker of 1952. The water at the downtown bridge was 13 feet 10 inches above the normal flow.

The Minneapolis Star (Minneapolis, Minnesota) reported that Walter Sturman, surveying the waters edging toward his house on appropriately named River Street, said ‘I’ve lived here all my 50 years and never seen it come up like this at this time of year.” Across the street, Allen Merriman was stacking cement blocks three high on his first floor. He planned to set his furniture on top, hoping the extra two feet would save it. “The water only came up 15 inches on the first floor in 1952,” he said. Next door, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Baldus had already evacuated but left their furniture behind. The water filled their basement. The home of “Tony” Boyce, Delano undertaker, stood like an island, its small parch of high ground completely surrounded by water.

Down in the center of town, the Rev. Andrew Hendzel, the pastor of St. Joseph’s Catholic church and head of the Red Cross unit in Delano, was directing operations in front of the Delano power plant. Boys of ages ranging from 8 and up worked side by side with the men to sandbag the river side of the building. Across the river, the town’s barber, Charles Bock, and his wife prepared to vacate their home behind his Main street shop at the edge of the bridge. Opening the trap door to the basement, Bock showed how all but two steps were below water. “It’s come up 7 inches in 7 hours,” said this 37-year resident of Delano. Across town on the north side, the Delano ballpark was under several feet of water. And nearby on Third Street abandoned homes included those of Richard Schultz, Elmer Witthum, Ralph Eggerglauss and Helmuth Schauer.

The St. Cloud Times reported that 35 families had been moved out.

This graphic air photo of Delano’s west side taken by Powell Krueger, Mpls. Star-Tribune staff photographer, shows the extent of the flooding before the flood crest was reached. In the lower left can be seen the transformer station and Leiter’s garage, both sandbagged against the flood waters. In the middle right can be seen the sandbag dike protecting the poser plant. The Wallisch garage directly across from the power plant was also sandbagged. To the left highway 12 can be seen as it disappears under three feet of water. Lowlands below town are also shown under water.
Flood of 1965
The most recent and severe flood in Delano occurred in April of 1965. Sudden warm temperatures and rain followed heavy snow that fell in March.. The Crow reached a crest of 18.4 feet in Delano.
The Crow River filled up the first floors of these houses along a residential section of north River Street. The river normally runs behind the houses, but had flooded nearly half of Delano.

The downtown businesses were also severely flooded. Sandbagging and pumping water out of their basements back over the dike saved many of the buildings. This picture was taken at the intersection of River Street and Elm Avenue.

Fire departments from surrounding towns, Watertown, Montrose, Long Lake, Maple Plain, and Mound provided valuable help maintaining the dike and pumping water. 25,000 sand bags were filled and used during the flood.
The dikes in the downtown area were about six feet high and as much as 20 feet thick. The flood waters were about two feet from the top of the dike.
On the river side of downtown, flooding was extensive.
The BoDo Café had 3 feet of water on the main floor.

The power plant flooded, and a Navy helicopter was necessary to rescue 5 men stranded in the facility: Leonard Logston, Milton Voltin, Darwin Voltin, George Schaar and Edward Libor. The helicopter also rescued two men who were stranded at the creamery: Joseph Schaust and Anthony Bauman. The waters were too high and the current too fast for boat rescues.
And once again, the Helmuth Schauer farm, on the north end of Central Park, was in the middle of the flood. Water was reported to be almost 10 feet deep in the village park.

On April 22, the Delano Eagle reported flood damage would exceed $1,000,000.00 in the village and the immediate surrounding area, as estimated by flood disaster personnel. The heart-breaking clean-up task that followed the record-breaking flood found people returning to their flooded homes to see floors covered with inches of oil-thick muck, warped beyond repair. Wallpaper hung loosely from the walls, and drains were plugged with muck. Furniture, if caught by the rising water, was scattered in disarray, and some buildings were moved on their foundations. Roads, driveways, and lawns were deeply gouged by the swirling torrents and over much of the flooded area were covered with a layer of rocks, sand, and silt. Debris was everywhere: parts of buildings, tree stumps, sings, logs, cans, fuel ranks, and an almost unbelievable amount of brush and weeds. The force of the torrent was graphically illustrated at the Granite Works highway display yard where monuments weighing up to a thousand pounds were tipped and scattered as though they were paper boxes. But as was the case during the actual flood, when help poured into the area from all over, offers came in to help in the cleanup task.

body.label: Delano on the Crow by John Bingea

body.html: Flood of 1969

High melt-off waters were predicted in March of 1969. The Delano Village Council had developed a plan to remove by ammonium-nitrate blasting, several Crow River sandbars which would slow the flow of water and impede floodwater runoffs. But what was really needed was a permanent solution to the flood problem. Delano applied for, and qualified for pre-disaster funds. Work began on March 20 on earthen dikes to protect Delano from the impending spring flood.

The Minnesota Highway Department in cooperation with the village of Delano and the U S. Corps of Engineers built 8,600 feet of dikes along both sides of the Crow River. Crews worked around the clock to complete the job by April 1. The diking and flood control project was possible with a $111,641 grant from the U. S. Corps of Engineers and an estimated expenditure of $50,000 by Delano. In addition, volunteers laid polyethylene and sandbags to keep the plastic in place on the dikes.

The Crow crested at 15.6, similar to that of the 1952 and 1957 floods, on April 11 1969, with the big news being that there was a lack of real damage done as compared to those former flood years. During the preceding week there had been constant dike patrols watching for wear and tear on the dikes, checking breaks, leaks and seepage, and constant pumping of those basements still filling with water.

In 2015, after over a century of flooding conditions which occasionally ravaged community homes and businesses, a flood containment system was installed along the river bank in order to protect the downtown district. It is comprised of a large underground footing system that supports removable walls which can be installed when needed.
High water March 23, 2019 caused the bridge to be closed, and the walls installed.

Ziebarth and Thomas Lebovsky, it has housed an ever-changing variety of businesses and residents through the decades, surviving changes in ownership, major floods, and the continuing evolution of downtown Delano.

In March of 1906, E. F. Ziebarth and Thomas Lebvosky advertised for bids from contractors for the erecting of a concrete or a solid brick building, 80x50 feet, two stories high with basement, in the village of Delano.  The  Delano Eagle reported in May that “E. F. Ziebarth and Thos. Lebovsky have had the plans drawn and have almost completed arrangements for the erection of a building on River Street immediately north of the telephone office. The new block will be of concrete, 50x80 feet two stories high with basement, with all modern improvements. Mr. Lebovsky will occupy his part of the building with his general store and the upper floor as dwelling rooms, while the basement of Mr. Ziebarth’s half will be occupied by Wm Cowle’s barber shop; the first floor by A. W. Kittock & Co’s. hardware store, and the second floor by the Northwestern Telephone Co. This new building will add another nice block to Delano’s row of business houses.”

If you look carefully at the photo, you can see the words “General Store” on the front of the first awning, and a barber pole at the basement entrance.

Thomas Lebvosky was still running his general store  business and living in his part of the building when he died in 1932.

Wermerskirchen & Co. purchased the stock of hardware owned by A. W. Kittock in 1910. The company, which was composed of Jacob Wermerskirchen and Peter Entinger of Minneapolis, intended to add more stock and in a short time have a complete line. Both gentlemen had been in business several years.

E.F. Ziebarth also owned the property next to the building, where he operated a farm machinery business.  Following the big delivery day of 24 International Harvester Company manure spreaders in October of 1914, the company of Ziebarth and Tomnitz treated their customers “right” by serving a fine dinner in the basement under Mr. Weihe’s hardware store.
The Marshall Wells store moved from its location across from City Hall to this building in 1939, occupying the north half of the building. This photo is from the 1951 DHS yearbook.

Roy Hanson opened his home bakery on Third and Elm in April of 1932, but moved downtown a few months later.  In 1946 Hanson’s Bakery was located next to the Marshall Wells store in the south half of the building, as reported in the Mainstreet, a special edition of the Eagle.

In 1965, this building housed a Red Owl Store, which was heavily damaged in the major flooding that occurred that spring.
The Red Owl store had from five to six feet of water standing in front of it in the street and about three feet of water on the main floor.
Several different restaurants have occupied the building since the 1970’s:
Lupine Brewing Company opened in the building after extensive renovation, restoration and remodeling in August of 2015.
Today, the building continues its long tradition of serving the community as home to Downtown Social, offering protein and energy drinks, and NorthStar Concierge Med/Family Practice.

stops.title: Bernick Building
stops.subtitle: Built 1885
stops.summary: Built in 1885 at 162 River Street North, the Bernick Building has stood at one of Delano’s busiest corners for more than 140 years. The site’s commercial history began in 1869 with John Borsch’s store and saloon, but after the original wooden building was destroyed by fire in 1885, the Bernick family replaced it with the handsome two-story brick building that remains today. Over the decades, the corner became especially well known for its saloons and taverns, including John Stein’s Corner Saloon and, beginning in 1941, the popular Main Bar. In 1956, the building became home to Delano Municipal Liquor, whose on-sale establishment was famously known as “The Zoo.” After the municipal liquor operation moved in 1983, the building served a variety of businesses and today continues its long commercial life as the home of Crow River Studio—preserving a landmark that has witnessed generations of change in downtown Delano.
